finding.claim: With caching enabled, a token that has exp (and/or nbf) but no numeric iat is cached without its expiry. The cached entry's validity window is set only by cacheTTL, so the token is still accepted from cache after it has expired. This is a business-logic and authorization flaw: an expired token stays valid for up to cacheTTL (default 600000 ms, 10 minutes).
finding.source: An attacker holds a validly signed JWT that has exp but no iat. This is common for tokens minted by third-party issuers or by a signer using noTimestamp. The attacker replays it after it expires, and the verifier was created with the cache option.
finding.sink: verify() returns the cached payload through handleCachedResult at src/verifier.js:377 instead of re-running the exp validator at src/verifier.js:319.

trace.note: A successful first verification calls cacheSet(cacheContext, payload).
hasIat is false because payload.iat is missing, so the whole block that reads nbf and exp is skipped.
Skipped when hasIat is false: cacheValue[1] (the nbf lower bound) stays 0.
Skipped when hasIat is false: cacheValue[2] is never set from payload.exp.
maxTTL is clockTimestamp + clockTolerance + cacheTTL. Because cacheValue[2] is 0, line 134 sets it to maxTTL, so the entry lives for the full cacheTTL regardless of exp.

On a later call the cache lookup runs before decoding and before any exp check. The check at lines 368-375 passes because min is 0 and now <= max, so the cached payload is returned at line 377 as valid even though exp is in the past.

finding.guards_checked: The verifyToken exp validator (src/verifier.js:304-323) runs only on a cache miss. The cache-hit time-range check (src/verifier.js:368-375) uses only the min and max values built in cacheSet. The ignoreExpiration and maxAge branches are nested inside the hasIat condition. No other expiry check exists on the cache-hit path.
